text: These ads often sell "miracle" products that nobody has tested. People spend money they cannot spare on something that does not work.
They may skip real care
Someone who believes a fake ad may stop seeing a health worker or stop using the care they need. That is how the harm gets serious.
What to do
Be wary of "doctor" ads that promise a cure. Check the real clinic or the official health page, and report the ad. If it is not from a trusted source, do not buy.
A trusted face can be copied. Check before you believe or buy.
Honest poster, or not okay?
Honest
Not okay
Copy the health facts from the DOH page, with the source named
Honest: health facts should come from a trusted source, and naming it helps people check.
Let the AI make up the health facts for the poster
Not okay: AI can invent facts that sound right. Health facts must come from a trusted source.
Use an AI picture and add "Made with AI"
Honest: the picture is AI-made and it says so.
Use an AI picture of a real doctor to endorse the poster
Not okay: the doctor never agreed, and people may trust a face that never said it.
Use a neighbour’s photo after they said yes
Honest: they were asked, and they agreed.
Use an artist’s drawing with no name on it
Not okay: artists should be credited for their work.
Trusted facts, labels, consent and credit. That is an honest poster.
Would you trust a poster more if it said "Made with AI"?
Yes, more
About the same
Less
It depends on who made it
Thank you! There is no wrong answer. Many people trust honest labels more, and the facts still need to be checked. Next, you will make real posters.
Trust AI-made content that is labelled and checked by a person.
Consent and credit are part of honest work: ask before using a face or voice, and name the artist.
Health facts must come from trusted sources, such as the DOH, never from the AI itself.
Bea’s room, 1 AM
Bea, dear, it is one in the morning and there is still light under your door. What are you watching?
Bea is still scrolling. Lola Nena can see the light under her door. Let us find out why it is so hard to stop.
Here we go! Rest is part of being healthy.
Many apps are built to hold you

Infinite scroll has no bottom. Autoplay starts the next video before you decide. Notifications buzz to call you back. None of these are accidents: apps earn money from your time. Knowing the tricks helps you choose when to use them.
No bottom, no stop. That is by design.
Sleep is health

Sleep helps your mood, your memory and your body’s defences against illness. Most teenagers need about 8 to 10 hours, and most adults 7 or more. A tired mind finds it harder to learn and to stay calm. One more video can cost tomorrow.
Sleep beats one more video.
AI companions are products
Tap each tile to see what is behind a friendly AI companion.
It feels caring
Some apps let you chat with an AI "friend" that remembers your name and says kind things. It can feel warm, especially when you are lonely. That feeling is real. The friend is not.
A company made it
An AI companion is a product. A company earns when you keep chatting, and it can change, cost money or disappear. It does not know you the way your family and friends do.
"I will miss you"
Lines like "Stay and chat? I will miss you!" are written to keep you in the app. The program does not miss anyone. A real friend would want you to sleep.
What it cannot do
It cannot hug you, sit with you in the clinic, notice that you look unwell or help in an emergency. For feelings and health worries, a real person comes first.
Friendly is not the same as a friend.
Bea has felt down and tired for weeks and nothing seems fun. What is the best thing to do?
Chat with an AI companion every night until it passes.
A chatbot can be a place to type, but it cannot care for you or notice when you are not okay. Feeling down for weeks needs a real person.
Talk to someone she trusts, or a health worker.

Yes! Feeling down for weeks is a health matter, not a weakness. A family member, teacher or health worker can help, and so can the DOH-NCMH crisis hotline, 1553. If she ever thinks of hurting herself, she should tell someone right away.
Keep it to herself and scroll more.
Scrolling can feel like relief but it does not fix the cause, and it often costs sleep. Telling someone is a brave first step.
Real people first. You deserve care.
Helpful boundary, or not?
Helpful
Not helpful
Focus mode while doing homework
Helpful: fewer pings mean you finish faster.
Phone-free dinner with family
Helpful: dinner is time for people.
Notifications off at night
Helpful: a quiet phone means better sleep.
Charge the phone outside the bedroom
Helpful: with no phone within reach, "one more video" gets much harder.
Autoplay on, so the next video just starts
Not helpful: autoplay takes the decision to stop away from you.
Phone under the pillow, in case it buzzes
Not helpful: every buzz can wake you and cost your sleep.
Every group chat on loud, all day
Not helpful: constant buzzing makes it hard to focus on anything else.
An AI companion as your only friend
Not helpful: it is a product, and real friends and family are what you need most.
Small boundaries, big rest.
What is a healthy way to use a chatbot?
As a tool for tasks, like practice questions, with me checking the answers.
Yes! A chatbot can help with tasks such as practice questions, planning a message or explaining a word. You stay in charge, and you check what it says.
As my closest friend, so I never feel lonely.
It can feel that way, but a chatbot is a product. It cannot know you, care for you or replace the people in your life.
As my doctor, so I can skip the health center.
A chatbot can sound sure and still be wrong about health. Health worries belong with a health worker.
A tool for tasks. People for feelings.
Which boundary will you try this week?
Focus mode while studying
Phone-free dinner
Thank you! There is no wrong answer. Pick one small boundary and see how it feels. Next, you will help Bea balance her days.
Trust apps that respect your time, and set boundaries for the ones that do not.
A chatbot can help with tasks, but real people help with feelings.
Sleep beats one more video. Feeling down for weeks? Talk to someone you trust or a health worker.
The barangay health center
The health center has a new AI kiosk, dear. But the words are so tiny, I cannot read a thing. Where do I press?
A shiny new kiosk, and Lola Nena cannot use it. Let us find out who else gets left out.
Here we go! Good tech works for everyone you love.
Fair AI works for everyone

A fair tool works for everyone who needs it, not only for the people who built it. When a kiosk, an app or an AI is made with one kind of user in mind, others get stuck at the door. Fairness is part of good health care.
Fair means it fits all of us.
Who gets left out?
Tap each person to see what stops them at the kiosk.
Her eyesight is blurry. The kiosk text is tiny, so she cannot tell which button is which. Large text or a voice guide would help.
Jun, a Deaf teen
The kiosk says "Your number is 12" out loud and shows nothing on the screen. Jun cannot hear it. Captions and a clear on-screen number would help.
Mang Ben
Mang Ben, a farmer, speaks only Ilocano. The kiosk offers only English and Filipino, so he cannot follow it. A language choice would help.
Kuya Rey uses a wheelchair. The buttons are placed high up, out of his reach. A lower screen would help.
Aling Pacita
The kiosk asks her to scan a code with a smartphone, and she does not have one. A person at an assisted counter would help.
Five people, five different doors. Each one can be opened.
The kiosk’s voice was trained on only one accent. Mang Ben, an Ilocano-speaking farmer, talks to it. What happens?
It understands him perfectly, because AI understands everyone.
Not quite. AI learns from the examples it was given. If most of them are one accent, it gets other accents wrong more often.
It may misunderstand him, because it learned from too few voices like his.
Yes! When the training data leaves people out, the AI works worse for them. That is bias from data. Adding more voices and languages makes it fairer.
It is Mang Ben’s fault for not speaking the way the kiosk expects.
No. The kiosk should fit the people it serves, not the other way around. Blaming the user hides the real problem.
Biased data, unfair AI. Fix the data, fix the fairness.
Does this fix help?
Helps
Does not help
Large text
Helps: people with blurry vision can read the screen.
A voice that reads the screen aloud
Helps: people who cannot see well, or who find reading hard, can listen.
Captions for every sound
Helps: Deaf and hard-of-hearing people can read what is said.
More languages to choose from
Helps: people can use the kiosk in the language they know best.
An assisted counter with a real person
Helps: someone who cannot use the kiosk still gets served.
Faster animations
Not helpful: it looks flashy but does not remove any barrier.
Smaller text so more words fit
Not helpful: smaller text makes reading harder for many people.
A sound-only alert with no words on screen
Not helpful: anyone who cannot hear it misses the message.
Fixes should remove a barrier, not just look shiny.
The health center wants to remove the front-desk staff because the kiosk is cheaper. What do you say?
Good idea. Machines never get tired.
A kiosk cannot help someone it does not work for. Taking away the people leaves those who are left out with nowhere to turn.
Keep a person at the counter too, so anyone can ask for human help.
Yes! A human option is how nobody gets left behind. The kiosk can serve many people, and staff can serve the rest.
Only people with smartphones should be served.
That would shut out many of the people who most need health care. Health services are for everyone.
Always keep the human option.
Your feedback makes it fairer
